New Parish space will be a hub for live music once again

The Oakland Theater Project will team up with Brooklyn Sound Lab to transform the storied building on San Pablo Avenue into a marquee music and performing arts center.
by Azucena Rasilla Nov. 11, 2026, 10:00 a.m.Nov. 10, 2026, 5:02 p.m.

Oakland’s music fans were in mourning late last year, when The New Parish, the iconic music venue on San Pablo Avenue that had helped launch the careers of artists from Kendrick Lamar to Fantastic Negrito to Bomba Estereo, announced that the venue had closed.

Now it turns out the space will become a music venue again, thanks to a new partnership between the Oakland Theater Project and Brooklyn Sound Lab.

The theater company — known for creatively reimagining  Shakespeare and other classics and staging original works that speak to the current social and political climate, and called “one of the most exciting young companies to emerge in the Bay Area in the past decade” by the San Francisco Chronicle — had long sought, managing director Colin Mandlin told The Oaklandside, a “more established performing space.”

“We’re committed to the city of Oakland. We want to be a staple of this community,” Mandlin said four years ago when the theater company celebrated its 10th anniversary.

That commitment became a reality on Oct. 22, when, after a seven-month process, the company announced it had leased — with a pre-negotiated option to purchase — the 13,000-square-foot building that had long been home to The New Parish, and before that the music venue Sweet Jimmie’s. Today the theater announced its new partnership with Brooklyn Sound Lab.

The theater had operated for years in surprising and nontraditional spaces, most recently a converted loading dock in what was the Flax art & design store in Uptown Oakland, the  company’s co-artistic director, William Hodgson, told The Oaklandside during an interview at the venue this week. “This is a historic opportunity,” he said. “It’s something I never thought would happen. But this is the dream that Michael [Moran, co-artistic director] and Colin and all of us set up so long ago, and with so many people’s work.”

Now, Mandlin and the team are engaged in an ambitious project to transform the space into a marquee performing arts center, and they knew that would mean bringing music shows back to the space. So Oakland Theater Project announced that it has teamed up with Ray and Melissa Archie, co-founders of Brooklyn Sound Lab, a sound design company based in Berkeley, to transform the venue’s acoustics and program musical performances there.

“The foundation of this collaboration is about how the building can still be the legacy beginning with Sweet Jimmie’s and continuing to the New Parish,” Ray Archie told The Oaklandside. “Thinking about 40-plus years of this building being important for the legacy of music in Oakland and the East Bay and the Bay Area in general, that goes from blues to rock to hip hop, to soul, to reggae, to world music.”

An opportunity to transform the space

The possibility for the space came at the perfect time, Mandlin said. The theater company was just ending its lease at the Flax building. 

“This is a big project, but it’s a dream project,” Mandlin told The Oaklandside. “It’s definitely something you can see throwing yourself into over the next five years, 10 years. There’s so much that we can start doing right away, and there’s so much we can build towards to make this place even more special than it already is.”

Mandlin said the team will begin by installing fixtures, a lighting grid, speakers and cabling to begin staging performances at the venue’s main stage — where music shows took place when it was The New Parish — by June 2027. Mandlin is working with the city to finalize permitting, which will determine the theater’s capacity inside the mainstage theater. But it’s likely to be more than the maximum capacity of 99 at their former home.

Ray Archie, a multi-instrumental musician and sound engineer, told The Oaklandside the company will begin teasing upcoming shows in December, though he won’t unveil the full 2027-2028 season until January.

He said he sees the renovations as “an opportunity to create and think about the acoustics of the space and put the audience within a more intimate environment. We are looking at how to transform this room to be better acoustically, to have more flexibility and diverse listening approaches and be one of the world class rooms here in the East Bay.”

The second phase of the project, Mandlin said, will involve enlarging the mainstage theater as well as developing the other parts of the space, including storefronts that were once home to the Rock Steady bar, Curry Up Now restaurant, Bicycle Coffee and Champion Sound Records.

According to Mandlin, the entrance to the former coffee shop will be the theater’s new entrance, complete with a lobby bar. The former restaurant and records shop will turn into a larger public lobby and restaurant that will open onto the courtyard, and the former bar will be transformed into a second, flexible performance space. 

Mandlin said the team is not ready to partner with any food vendors quite yet but is already at work trying to obtain a liquor license. By the time the new season opens at the new venue, he said, the plan is to have drinks and concessions.

“To be able to do two venues is just special for us. I think it’s special for Oakland,” Mandlin said. “I think it’s going to be a gem of the Bay Area.”

A music partnership rooted in love for The Town

Born and raised in Oakland, Ray Archie is a music virtuoso who, when he was young, played with the Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra, the Berkeley Youth Orchestra and the San Francisco Symphony Youth Orchestra. He is a classically-trained musician who has toured with the likes of Leonard Bernstein, Michael Tilson-Thomas and the San Francisco Symphony. He is also a sound engineer who once worked as the director of streaming operations for CBS radio. A decade ago, he and his wife Melissa joined forces to found Brooklyn Sound Lab in New York, eventually relocating the business to the Bay. The pair describe themselves as “sound alchemists” and have specialized in theatrical sound design, scores and audiobook production.

Archie said he’s excited to transform the space’s acoustics and bring programming into a building where he has many deep connections, dating back to his family’s ties with the family of Jimmy Ward, who owned Sweet Jimmie’s. Both families, he said, migrated from Louisiana and four members of the two families worked alongside one another as longshoremen in Oakland.

Archie said he and Mandlin began working together four years ago, when Mandlin brought on Archie as the sound designer — and sometimes the composer and music director — for many of the company’s theater productions. Archie has worked with Oakland Theater Project on “Cabaret,” “Angels in America,” and “I Am My Own Wife,” among other productions.

Now, Archie and Mandlin are collaborating on the larger vision for the space.

“The Public Theater and Joe’s Pub are a very interesting model that we’re looking at,” Archie said, speaking of the adjoining theater and cabaret venue in Manhattan. “A highly curated, diverse experience where both our audience and our artists have a white glove treatment.”

Archie said he and Mandlin envision booking homegrown artists, as well as touring musicians from all genres. 

Mandlin will continue managing the theater company, while the Archies will be in charge of the music side of this venture. Melissa Archie said she will handle sponsorships, community collaborations, media relations and audience experience.

“Much of my career in music, media, and entertainment in New York has centered on building relationships and connecting with audiences,” she said. “I want to help create a space where people feel equally welcome, where audiences discover something unexpected, and where the experience goes beyond what’s happening on stage.”

“Oakland deserves a space that feels like it belongs to the community, where people feel seen, welcomed, and inspired to participate,” she said.

A big project — with a big fundraising goal

Mandlin didn’t want to say how much it will cost the theater to buy the building and undertake the significant renovations the team has in mind. He did say that longtime supporters of the organization have shared their excitement about what the building could look like in a few years, and have pledged their support for the endeavor. 

“We are trying to be smart along the way, and not overcommit,” Mandlin said. “Long term, when we do have the two theater spaces, the amount of main stage productions and experimental shows that we take on will increase,” providing an opportunity for more revenue.

Archie also sees a revenue opportunity in opening up the building for daytime programming, expanding beyond theater and music shows.

“We are looking for creative ways of staying engaged with the local music community,” Archie said. “Looking at a series of educational workshops, Sunday matinee type events in different areas of the space. It’s a large building, so we don’t have to go dark….It’s about activating the space consistently.”

As Archie begins to program the venue for next year, he describes the opportunity as a “dream come true.”

“I think every musician or engineer wants to have a live music venue,” Archie said. “This is a dream to have a team that I can really go deep with and create transformation, as well as impact the local community.”

Colin said it’s a major turning point for Oakland Theater Project, especially at a time when performance venues are in decline.

“It is a sigh of relief that we get to put down roots in a way where we have financial and physical stability for the decades to come,” Mandlin said. “We’ve always celebrated wanting to bring the exquisite theater that we know how to create to life, but also wanting to uplift and help to produce and promote other artists and other art forms — and with this building, wanting to continue the legacy of incredible music and dance there.”


Thank you for reading to the end – truly.

azucena@oaklandside.org

Azucena Rasilla, The Oaklandside’s arts and community reporter, joined the newsroom in June 2020. A bilingual journalist from East Oakland, she has reported on Oakland arts, culture and community for over a decade. She regularly hosts Oaklandside Culture Makers, a quarterly live event that highlights Oakland creatives. She started her career at the East Bay Express and her work has appeared in the San Francisco Chronicle, KQED, Eater and Curbed.
